items.item: CSR is not merely 'an adjacency list flattened into one array' — it is the row-compressed form of the same offsets+column-index layout used for sparse matrices in numerical computing (cuSPARSE's own CSR description), so the format this topic teaches is identical, not analogous, to the one used in sparse linear algebra libraries.

CSC is not a separately-built structure; it has exactly the same memory layout as CSR's transpose. So building CSC for reverse-edge queries is correctly framed as 'transpose the construction', not as a second, independent representation to learn.
items.placement: here — CSC named for reverse edges (topic 37)

items.item: Reverse Cuthill-McKee is a permutation computed over a graph already in CSR/CSC form, not a separate graph structure — the function signature itself (scipy.sparse.csgraph.reverse_cuthill_mckee takes a CSR/CSC matrix and returns a permutation array) is itself evidence that reordering composes with, rather than replaces, the representation.

The real motivation for reordering at all is a specific, measured number, not a vague 'locality is good': cache miss latency (not CPU compute) is the majority of graph-processing time in prior measurement, which is why a representation change alone (adjacency list to CSR) is not the whole story — the vertex numbering on top of it is a second, independent lever on the same bottleneck.

A degree-sort-only reordering is not strictly dominant over no reordering: it improves temporal locality (hot, high-degree vertices stay cache-resident) but can actively hurt spatial locality for neighbourhood-walking algorithms like BFS, which is the real, sourced reason the syllabus names three different reordering strategies (degree sort, BFS/RCM, community order) instead of just 'sort by degree' — each targets a different one of these two locality types.
items.placement: here — motivates naming BFS/RCM and community order as real alternatives, not just more options (topic 37)

items.item: CSR's two-pass build from an edge list (count degrees -> prefix sum into offsets, then scatter into targets using a per-vertex write cursor) is the reason topic 36 built the edge list first: CSR's natural input is an edge list, not an adjacency list, so the dependency direction in the chapter plan (36 before 37) is structurally required, not just a pedagogical choice.
